title: The Cups at Bangaon
teaser: In a 1971 refugee camp, a doctor short of drips handed cholera treatment to patients' families. Their cups of salty, sugary water worked.
story: In 1971, the war that created Bangladesh drove an estimated 10 million refugees out of what was then East Pakistan and into camps along the Indian border. Cholera followed them. At Bangaon, in West Bengal, one camp's health centre was run by Dilip Mahalanabis, a 36-year-old paediatrician from the Johns Hopkins International Center for Medical Research and Training in Calcutta.

Cholera kills by draining water and salt from the body. The standard treatment was intravenous fluid, dripped straight into a vein, and in the camps it was in short supply. So Mahalanabis began giving a drink instead to every patient who was not in urgent need of a drip. His team packed glucose, salt and baking soda into packets, each enough for a litre of water.

Trained health workers did not hand it out. According to a 2001 WHO account, 'mothers, sisters, spouses, grandmothers and friends collected the solution in small cups from central drums and dosed their suffering family members.' Staff kept the drums filled and made quick rounds of the patients. Families asked for 'saline', the treatment they trusted, so Mahalanabis called the drink 'oral saline'.

The idea he was testing is oral rehydration therapy: replacing lost fluid by mouth with a measured solution of water, salt and sugar. The sugar is not there for energy. The gut absorbs sugar actively, and sodium travels in with it, so the salt and water the body needs are drawn in too. Researchers in Dhaka and Calcutta had shown in the late 1960s, in hospital trials, that it could work as well as a drip. Bangaon tested it in a crisis, in untrained hands.

The results were stark. Cholera patients in Mahalanabis's camp died at a rate of about 3 per cent, against 20 to 30 per cent in camps that relied on intravenous fluid alone. Some journals turned his paper down because they did not find the figures credible; it appeared in the Johns Hopkins Medical Journal in 1973. In 1978, the year the World Health Assembly launched a global programme against diarrhoeal disease with oral rehydration at its heart, The Lancet called the treatment 'potentially the most important medical advance' of the century.
A course now costs around 50 US cents in poorer countries. The hard part at Bangaon was not the chemistry but trusting families to give it, and that is still where many lives are won or lost.
takeaway: Oral rehydration therapy: replacing the fluid lost in diarrhoea by drinking a measured solution of water, salt and sugar, because sugar helps the gut absorb salt and, with it, water. At Bangaon in 1971, families giving it from cups cut cholera deaths to about 3 per cent.

recall.question: In 1970s Bangladesh, Muhammad Yunus lent tiny sums to villagers in Jobra who had nothing to offer as security. What is the lending idea called, and what took the place of collateral?
recall.answer: Solidarity lending: borrowers are put in small groups whose members share a stake in each other's repayment, so neighbours' knowledge and social ties stand in for security.

rabbitHole.title: Salt, sugar and the second-class cure
rabbitHole.intro: Why can't any salty, sugary drink do the job, how does sugar pull water into the body, and why did the recipe change thirty years on? Down we go.

levels.heading: Not just salty water
body: The popular version is that oral rehydration is simply salt and sugar in water. The evidence says the proportions matter. The original WHO solution contained 90 mmol of sodium per litre, with a total osmolarity of 311 mOsm per litre, and a 2002 WHO and UNICEF statement added that glucose 'should not exceed 111 mmol/l'.

Getting those proportions right in the field was its own problem. Dhiman Barua, a WHO cholera specialist who visited Mahalanabis at Bangaon in 1971, later recalled that at the end of 1970 a Swiss company succeeded in packaging the ingredients in aluminium foil bags. He also recalled the resistance. 'Hospital doctors regarded oral rehydration therapy as a second-class treatment,' he said, and paediatricians in rich countries feared the sodium was too high for small children.

levels.heading: Why sugar opens the door
body: The trick rests on a piece of gut physiology. Experiments on animals showed that glucose enhances the absorption of sodium and water across the lining of the intestine. The cells of the gut wall actively take up sugar, and the work of Robert Crane and others showed that sodium in the gut is essential to that process. As sugar and sodium move into the cells, water and chloride follow.

According to a 1994 history by S. K. Bhattacharya, Captain Phillips of the US Army first gave oral glucose saline successfully to two cholera patients in 1964. Teams at the Cholera Research Laboratory in Dhaka and the Infectious Diseases Hospital in Calcutta then turned it into a standard solution, and N. F. Pierce and others showed in 1965 to 1969 that it worked.

levels.heading: Less salt, thirty years on
body: In May 2002, WHO and UNICEF told countries to replace the old formula with a weaker one. The new solution has 75 mmol of sodium and 75 mmol of glucose per litre, with a total osmolarity of 245 mOsm per litre. A litre's worth of powder holds 2.6 g of sodium chloride, 13.5 g of glucose, 1.5 g of potassium chloride and 2.9 g of trisodium citrate.

The evidence came from trials in children with diarrhoea other than cholera. The need for unplanned intravenous drips fell by 33 per cent, and pooled studies of similar solutions found stool output down by about 20 per cent and vomiting down by about 30 per cent. There was one caution: in adults with cholera the new drink worked as well as the old but brought more cases of brief, symptom-free low blood sodium, so monitoring was advised. When the UN publicised the new formula in 2006, it also pointed to zinc: 20 mg a day for 10 to 14 days, with continued breastfeeding, helps protect against dehydration.

lookingGlass.heading: How many lives, really?
body: That the drink works is not in serious doubt. What is less certain is the famous count of lives saved. Our World in Data's widely quoted figure of around 70 million since the late 1970s is its own extrapolation from a 2007 BMJ estimate of more than 50 million children saved between 1982 and 2007, and the site itself says the exact number is 'impossible to know', because other improvements in child health were happening at the same time. Dhiman Barua made the same point: oral rehydration 'may not be solely responsible' for the fall in child deaths from diarrhoea.
There is a practical limit too. The drink does not stop diarrhoea; it replaces what is lost. Parents judging it by whether the diarrhoea stops can give up on it too soon.
lookingGlass.verdict: Where that leaves you: trust the treatment, which has strong trial evidence behind it, but treat the big lives-saved totals as informed estimates rather than counts.

quiz.question: At the Bangaon refugee camp in 1971, who gave most cholera patients their oral fluid?
options: Their relatives, using small cups filled from central drums
Nurses flown in by the World Health Organization
The patients themselves, from bottles bought at the camp shop
quiz.explain: Mothers, sisters, spouses, grandmothers and friends collected the solution in cups from central drums, while staff kept the drums filled and checked on patients.

quiz.question: Why does oral rehydration solution contain sugar?
options: The gut absorbs sugar actively, and sodium and water are drawn in with it
To give a weak patient enough energy to recover
To hide the taste of the salt so children will drink it
To kill the cholera bacteria in the gut
quiz.explain: The sugar is not there for energy. Sodium travels into the gut wall with sugar, and the water the body needs follows.
